title: The chariot of fire (2 Kings 2:1–14)
hookLine: Elisha won't leave Elijah and asks for a double portion of his spirit

cards: Two men are on the road out of Gilgal, an old prophet and his student. Elijah stops and says, "Tarry here, I pray thee." Stay here; the LORD has sent me on to Bethel.

At Bethel, a company of prophets asks Elisha: don't you know the LORD will take your master from you today? His answer is short: "Yea, I know it; hold ye your peace." And Elijah says it again: tarry here.

teach.h: I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE, THREE TIMES.
teach.b: Three times Elijah tells him to stay behind: at Gilgal, at Bethel, at Jericho. Three times Elisha gives the same answer, in the King James words: "As the LORD liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee."
They walk on to the Jordan. Elijah takes his mantle, his cloak, rolls it up, and strikes the water, and it parts, and they cross on dry ground.
Across the river, Elijah turns to him: "Ask what I shall do for thee, before I be taken away from thee."

teach.h: A DOUBLE PORTION OF THY SPIRIT.
teach.b: Elisha doesn't ask small: "I pray thee, let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me."
Some readers hear an echo of the law in Deuteronomy, where the firstborn son receives a double portion: Elisha is asking to be his heir. Elijah is honest: "Thou hast asked a hard thing."
But if you see me when I'm taken, it will be yours.

teach.h: A WHIRLWIND, AND A CHARIOT BETWEEN.
teach.b: As they walk, a chariot of fire and horses of fire come between them, "and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven." The text is exact here: the chariot parted them, and the whirlwind took him up.
Elisha cries out, "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof." He tears his own clothes in two.

teach.h: WHERE IS THE LORD GOD OF ELIJAH?
teach.b: Then he picks up the mantle that fell from Elijah, walks back to the Jordan, and strikes the water with it, asking, "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" The water parts.
The one who wouldn't leave is the one left holding the mantle. He stayed to the end, he asked plainly, and he saw.

how: Some Christians speak of 'passing the mantle' when one generation of leaders hands on to the next, and some churches echo Elisha's request for a double portion when they pray for new leaders.

games.q: you're Elisha. your teacher says: tarry here, I pray thee. everyone seems to know he's about to be taken away. what do you do?
o: as the LORD liveth, I will not leave thee.
go ahead of him and wait at the river.
games.why: three times he refuses to leave. at the Jordan he asks plainly for a double portion, sees Elijah taken, and is left holding the mantle.

practice: Think of someone who taught you how to live, or work, or believe: a parent, a coach, a pastor.
If they're still here, ask yourself what you'd want to ask of them, plainly, before it's too late; if they're gone, ask what mantle they left in your hands. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Mantle. Elijah's cloak, which parted the Jordan and then fell to Elisha, who refused to leave his teacher and asked for a double portion of his spirit.

orig.note: Hebrew: a cloak or mantle; Elijah's mantle parts the Jordan, and then falls to Elisha (2 Kings 2:8, 2:13).

carryVoice: Your line: I will not leave you. A week from a kingdom torn in two, through ravens, a widow's jar, Carmel, a broom tree and a stolen vineyard, to a chariot of fire. A full week.
